items.title: FREE Mode Coder: This is LITERALLY $0 - NO SUBSCRIPTION FREE CODER!
items.summary:
Visit Verdent: https://www.verdent.ai/?id=700712

In this video, I'll be showing you how to use Verdent Free mode, which gives everyone access to an AI coding agent without requiring a subscription or credits. I'll walk through the setup, test it on a JavaScript shopping-cart bug, and explain the differences between Free, Eco, and Prime modes.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Verdent Free mode is now available to everyone without a paid subscription or credits.
🛠️ Free mode can inspect project files, edit code, run commands, and verify its changes.
🧪 In the coding test, Verdent fixed a JavaScript cart calculation and passed all five existing tests.
⏳ The Free allowance refreshes every five hours and is also subject to a weekly usage cap.
💸 Free requires no subscription, Eco uses zero credits with a subscription, and Prime spends credits.
📂 Free mode is available through regular project tasks, while Manager currently supports Eco and Prime.
💡 Focused bug fixes, code explanations, small interface c
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Verdant has opened free mode to everyone. And this is a pretty interesting update if you want an AI coding agent without adding another subscription to your monthly expenses. You can open the desktop app, choose free mode, and start working without buying a subscription or credits. There is an allowance that refreshes, and there is also a weekly cap, which I'll explain in a bit. But the part I wanted to check was what you can actually do with it, because having a free option is useful when it can get through a task you care about. So, in this video, I'll show you how to start using it, walk through a small coding test I ran in the desktop app, and explain how free is different from eco and prime. I'll also talk about the kinds of tasks I would try first if I were using this on a limited budget. So, let's get right into it. If you haven't used Verdant before, it's an AI coding tool where you open a project and describe what you want done. The agent can work with the files in that project, make changes, and run commands to check the result. For example, you can give it a bug to investigate and ask it to reproduce the problem before making a change. You can then look at the files it edited and the tests it ran, all as part of the same task. That is the workflow we're going to use here. I want to see whether it can read a small piece of code, understand why it is broken, fix it, and verify the fix. Now, the 2.13 update also changed how you choose the AI for a task. You have free, eco, and prime, and Verdant can route the task automatically based on the mode you select. Personally, I like having this option. When you're just trying to fix something small, choosing between a bunch of model names can become another decision before you've even started working. Here, we can select free and get on with the task. In the desktop app, the description says basic models for light work, which gives you a reasonable idea of where to start. Now, let me show you the setup. First, download Verdant from its official website, install the desktop app, and sign in. Once you're inside, go to projects and click new task. You'll see the option to select or create a project. For this example, I'm choosing an existing folder because I've already prepared a small project with the code and its tests. Then, beside the message box, open the mode selector and choose free. You can see that it is selected here. Now, you can type your request and send it. One detail to keep in mind is that I'm using a regular project task. Manager currently supports eco and prime. So, if you're following this particular free mode walk-through, start from projects and new task as I'm going here. Anyway, let's come to the example. I have a tiny JavaScript shopping cart function. Its job is to take some items, multiply their prices by their quantities, and return the total. The problem is that values coming from a form can arrive as text. So, a price that looks like $12.50 might actually be stored as a string, and the original function just adds that value to the running total. With strings, JavaScript can end up joining the text together. The function also ignores the quantity, which means buying three of something doesn't produce the correct total, either. This gives us a straightforward problem with a result we can check. If one item costs $12.50 and I buy two, the total should be $25. I've also included five tests. They cover values coming in as strings, multiple items, ordinary numeric values, a small decimal calculation, and an empty cart. Before the fix, four of those tests fail. Only the empty cart test passes because the function starts with zero and has nothing to add. So, here's what I'm asking Verdin to do. Fix the cart total calculation. Prices and quantities may arrive as strings from a form. Return a number rounded to cents, and return zero for an empty cart. Run the existing tests first, make the smallest fix, and run them again. Leave the test file unchanged. I also tell it to keep the work inside this project and avoid adding dependencies because this example should only need a small change to the calculation. I think this is a useful way to write these prompts. You're giving the agent the problem, the expected behavior, and a way to check its work. It has enough information to act without having to guess what success looks like. So, let's send it and see. Okay, it starts by exploring the project files. Then it runs the existing tests and reproduces the failures. You can see it reports that four out of five tests are failing. Next, it edits the function and runs the tests again. And now all five pass. I also re-ran the tests separately after it finished and got the same result. Five passed, zero failed. So, that's great. Now, if we open the change, it's pretty easy to follow. It converts the price and quantity into numbers, multiplies them together for each item, and adds the result to the total. Then it rounds the final result to cents. The change is two lines in the function. The test file stays the same. That last part matters because we're checking the fix against the expectations we started with. The string inputs now produce a number. Quantities are included. And the empty cart still returns zero. For the multi-item example, two items at $12.50 plus another item at $5.25 now give us $30.25. That matches the expected result. So, this is a useful result from free mode. It handled the file reading, the test run, the edit, and the verification in one request. Now, this is a small prepared example. It shows how free mode handled this particular bug. And I'd want to try more demanding tasks before judging its performance on a large project. But for this focus change, it did what I asked. Let's talk about the allowance next because this is something you should understand before planning your work around it. According to Veridant, free mode refreshes every 5 hours and also has a weekly cap. So, you have both a shorter usage window and a limit across the week. That weekly cap still applies even though the shorter allowance refreshes. Keep both in mind if you're planning several sessions over a few days. The announcement doesn't give a fixed number of messages, so I wouldn't tell you that everyone gets a particular number of prompts. Check the usage information in your app as you work, especially before starting something that might need several rounds of changes. For me, that makes focus tasks a sensible starting point. If I already have an error message and a clear expected result, I can put those in the first request. That gives the agent useful context immediately and can save some back and forth. Now, let's also clear up the difference between free and eco because the zero credit wording can make these sound similar. Free is available without subscribing. Eco also costs zero credits, but requires a subscription and has its own quota. Prime spends credits for access to stronger models. So, when you're trying Verdin without a paid plan, choose free. If you already subscribe, eco is another option to consider for your work. And with prime, the credit cost becomes part of the decision. I would look at the result I'm getting before deciding to move up. If a focus task is being handled well, that's useful information. If I keep getting incomplete changes or spending several attempts correcting the same misunderstanding, then I would reassess the task, the prompt, and the mode I'm using. Anyway, beyond this demo, there are a few other kinds of tasks I would try with free mode. The first is understanding unfamiliar code. Maybe you've downloaded a small project and you're trying to figure out where a form submission goes. I'd ask the agent to trace that flow and explain the relevant files before changing anything. That gives you something specific to check. You can open the files it mentions and follow the explanation. If you're learning, you can then ask about the particular part you don't understand. Another task I'd try is a small clearly described interface change. Maybe a button label is confusing or an empty state needs a better explanation. I'd give it the exact wording and point it at the relevant part of the project. For that kind of change, I'd open the app afterward and check it on screen. A passing test doesn't tell you whether text is getting cut off or whether the result looks right at a smaller window size. Documentation is another possibility. Once a small feature is working, I might ask it to explain how to run it, what inputs it expects, and how to run the tests. Then, I'd follow those instructions myself to see whether someone new could actually use them. Those are examples I would explore next. The test we actually ran today was the cart calculation, and that's the result I'm basing this demonstration on. The useful habit is to decide how you'll check the outcome before sending the request. For our cart example, we had expected totals, existing tests, and a change small enough to inspect. If [snorts] you're a student working through a small project, that also gives you an opportunity to learn from the fix. After checking that it works, look at why it works. In our example, understanding the difference between adding numbers and joining strings is something you can use elsewhere in JavaScript. And if you already code regularly, I'd use the same approach to evaluate how much help it gives you. Try a task you'd otherwise handle yourself, inspect the output, and see whether the time saved is meaningful for your workflow. Overall, I like that you can now try this without making a subscription decision first. The small bug fix worked, the changes were easy to inspect, and we got the expected test results. The allowance will matter if you're using it frequently, and the scope of your tasks will matter, too. But if you want to experiment with an AI coding agent on a small project, this is a pretty good place to start. I'll leave Verdens website and the announcement in the description so you can check it out and read the current terms yourself. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks [music] option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music] [music]

items.title: /GRAFT Skill + Astra: THIS IS ABSOLUTELY CRAZY!
items.summary:
In this video, I’ll show you how Graft works with Verdent to help AI coding agents understand codebases more efficiently. We’ll build a structural code graph, investigate a permissions bug, trace function relationships, apply a fix, refresh the graph, and verify everything with tests.

--
Key Takeaways:

🧠 Graft builds a queryable code graph containing functions, imports, and relationships across your project.
🔑 The structural graph works without an AI provider key or a separate database server.
🤖 Verdent can use the Graft CLI to investigate code, inspect files, make edits, and run tests.
🔍 Graft queries and skeleton views help agents find implementations, inspect APIs, and trace function callers.
🐛 In the demo, Graft helps identify a missing export permission check in a document service.
🔄 Graft can detect stale graph data and automatically refresh changed files after an edit.
✅ The final tests confirm that viewers can still read documents but cannot export them without permission.
📊
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. So, if you use AI coding agents, you have probably seen this happen. You open a project, ask for a small fix, and the agent spends the next few minutes searching files, reading imports, and figuring out how everything connects. Then, you start another task, and it does a lot of that work again. Today I want to show you an open source project called Graph that tries to make that process more efficient. It builds a code graph that your agent can query so it has a better starting point when it needs to understand your project. And for this video I actually installed it and used it through Verdant. I prepared a small document service with a permissions bug ran the tests and asked Verdant to investigate it using Graph. So we have a concrete example to look at along with the commands and outputs you can reproduce yourself. So let's get right into it. First, what does graft actually do? It reads the source code and records things like functions, imports, and the connections between them. You can ask where something is implemented, look at a files available functions, or trace which parts of the project call a particular function. That information is useful because a coding task usually involves more than finding one matching word. If I change a permissions function, I also want to know which services use it. And if a service behaves incorrectly, I want to follow the path that led to that behavior. Now, graft has two layers and this is an important distinction. The basic build uses tree sitter to analyze code structure. You can build the graph and run the queries we are using today without giving graph an AI provider key. There is also an optional deep build which adds AI written summaries and concept nodes that uses your configured model provider. So there can be API costs depending on the provider you choose. We are using the structural layer in this demo. All the results you will see here work without that additional model call. The project is MIT licensed and the structural graph does not require a separate database server. It keeps its generated files inside a graft folder in your project. The build also adds that folder to git ignore because you can regenerate it from the code. So the basic setup is quite approachable, but free graft queries do not make the coding agent itself free. If your agent or model has usage charges, those still apply. Keep those two costs separate. Now I have Verdant open here. The basic workflow is to open a project folder, create a task, and describe what you want the agent to do. It can inspect files, edit the code, and run terminal commands with the progress and results shown in the task. You also have a model selector and there is plan mode when you want to work through an approach before implementation. For this example, the requirements are already clear. So I'm giving the agent a specific investigation to carry out. Verdant also gives you file views and change summaries. So once the agent edits something, you can inspect what changed. There is a code review feature as well. And for larger work, its manager can break a goal into subtasks and coordinate workers. One thing to keep in mind is that tasks in the same workspace share the files. Creating another task does not automatically mean every edit is isolated. For this walkthrough, I opened a dedicated demo folder which keeps the example easy to follow. Now, Graph does not currently have a dedicated Verdant entry in its integration installer. What we are doing here is asking Verdant to run the Graph CLI. Verdant also supports MCP and Graph has an MCP server, but the integration I actually tested for this video is the command line workflow. First, I asked Verdant to check the node version and install graft locally. The version I tested is 0.18.0 and it requires node 20 or newer. My machine was running node 22. For a quick setup on your own machine, you can use npx with the at nanonets/graph package. For the recording, I pinned the version and installed it in a separate tooling folder so we can repeat the same example. I have put the exact commands in the companion notes. Once that is installed, we can run graft build inside the code repository. There is no provider key to enter for this part. I also disabled optional telemetry for the demo commands. Now let's look at the example. This is a small document service with owners, editors, viewers, and unrelated users. A viewer should be able to read a shared document, but exporting it as a CSV file should require an editor or owner. These are rules for our sample app. A different product could choose a different export policy. The point is to see whether the code follows the policy we have actually defined. So let's run the baseline tests. We have nine tests, eight pass and one fails. The failing test says a viewer cannot export a shared document but the handler returns status 200 instead of 403. And if we run the example directly, we can see the same thing. The viewer can read, which is expected. The viewer cannot edit, which is also expected. But the viewer can export the document, which is the bug we put into this fixture. I like using a small example like this because you can follow the entire path. It is synthetic data and we are calling the route handlers locally. There is no production account or deployed service involved. Now for the first graft example, let's understand the codebase. Verdant runs graft build and it produces 29 nodes and 66 edges from nine JavaScript files including the tests. Those numbers are from this tiny fixture so they are not a scalability benchmark. Then we run graft map to get an overview and ask where document export permissions are checked. We add the d- source flag. So the results include the relevant code alongside the file locations. Okay. The first result is the export document function. The next result is the export permission helper. We also get the export route handler and the function that loads a document for a user. That is a useful collection of files for this question. We can see the export function fetching the document and immediately turning it into CSV. We can also see a separate helper that permits owners and editors to export. Graph is returning relevant source here. Verdant is still responsible for reading that source and reasoning about whether the behavior is correct. The query itself is deterministic retrieval. So we are not paying another model just to produce these search results. There is also the skeleton command. We run it on the permissions file and it lists the function signatures for checking a document's role. Read permission, edit permission, and export permission. That gives us a quick overview of the files API without dumping every function body into the conversation. Now for the second example, let's follow the callers. We ask graph which parts of the project call the export document function with a depth of two. It shows the route handler and then the connections to the demo and test. Then we ask the same thing about the export permission helper. And here is the useful clue. The output points to the tests, but there is no call from the export service. So the policy exists and there is even a test checking that policy directly. But the actual export path never uses it. This is why testing a helper alone is not enough. The helper can be correct while the feature using it is still broken. If we follow the source, the export service loads the document through a function that checks read access. A viewer passes that check because viewers are allowed to read. The export service then creates the CSV without checking the stricter export permission. That explains both the failing test and the missing connection in the graph. So we have something concrete for the agent to fix. Now I ask Verdant to enforce the existing export policy inside the export service. The change is small. Import the permission helper. Import the error type and reject the request if the user cannot export. We keep the existing tests exactly as they are. And here is the third example which I think is quite useful. After the edit, we run graph check before rebuilding anything. It reports that the graph is stale and identifies the export service has changed. Then we run the same graft question again without manually running another build. The output says it refreshed the graph because one file changed and the source excerpt now includes the new permission check. If we ask for the callers of the export permission helper again, the export document function now appears. So we can see the connection that was missing before the fix. A subsequent freshness check reports that the graph is current. This matters when an agent is making several changes in a session. You want its next query to reflect the updated code. In this run, that worked with an uncommitted edit. And I also repeated the sequence in a separate temporary copy to verify it. Now, let's run the tests again. All nine pass. The viewer gets 403 when trying to export. While the editor can still export successfully, the viewer can still read the document, too. So, we have kept the intended read access. So, that's great. The graph helped us find and inspect the relevant connection and the tests verified the resulting behavior. I would still keep both parts of that workflow. A graph showing the new call does not by itself prove the implementation is correct. Graph also has an interactive visualization. I exported the code graph and opened it inside Verden's browser panel. You can switch between the graph and a file outline. Select a function and inspect what it depends on and what depends on it. I have included both the before and after exports with the examples. Now there are a few limitations to keep in mind. Static analysis has limits especially with dynamic behavior and graph's language support varies in depth. The graph is useful context but you still need to inspect the code when the result is ambiguous. The automatic refresh we tested update structure. It does not regenerate paid AI summaries every time you ask a question. If a refresh fails, graph can fall back to the existing graph. So pay attention to its notices. And if you want the deep layer, make sure it actually ran with your configured provider. A successful command alone does not prove those summaries were generated. You will also see token- saving estimates in some graph outputs. Those compare the returned context with reading the covered files in full. They are estimates and they do not prove that our complete Verdant session used that percentage fewer tokens. The maintainers separately report 42% fewer tokens and 60% less time in their controlled benchmark. Those are their results. This small walk through verifies the commands and the bug fix workflow. It does not reproduce that benchmark or establish a speed up over using Verdant alone. For Verdant's pricing, the current monthly options start at $5 for light. Starter is $19, pro is $59, and max is $179. The pricing page also lists 100 free credits valid for 7 days for new users. Check the current limits and model costs when you choose a plan. Personally, I think Graph is worth trying when your agent repeatedly needs to understand relationships across a codebase. You can start with a structural graph, use a few targeted queries, and see whether the results help on your actual project before setting up the optional deep layer. And Verdant gives us a convenient place to run that workflow, inspect the output, review the changes, and keep the tests alongside the task. The complete example includes the original failing version, the fixed version, the graph exports, and a replay script that runs the sequence in a temporary copy. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. [music] If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the [music] join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. [music] >> [music]

items.title: FULLY FREE Deepseek V4.1 Flash Coder: This SHOULDN'T BE FREE! (+My Design Workflow)
items.summary:
In this video, I’ll show you how to try DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for coding through WorkBuddy’s international app during its two-week free-access promotion. I’ll also use it to build a design studio portfolio and a creator analytics dashboard with the Impeccable design skill.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is available to try through WorkBuddy with zero-credit pricing during the limited-time offer.
🛠️ You can use the model without configuring your own DeepSeek API key.
🎨 DeepSeek can generate polished frontend prototypes from a clear visual brief.
🖼️ The Forma portfolio includes custom vector artwork, project filters, responsive layouts, and theme switching.
📊 The Signal dashboard includes interactive charts, range controls, table search, and light and dark themes.
✨ WorkBuddy supports design skills such as Impeccable for better typography, spacing, responsiveness, and visual hierarchy.
🔄 Reviewing the generated interface and providing specific feedback can significantly improve
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, if you wanted to try Deep Seek V4.1 Flash for coding without paying for another subscription, there's a pretty interesting option available right now. Work Buddy has added the model to its international app, and they're advertising it as free to try for 2 weeks. And the reason I wanted to cover this is that Deep Seek is getting really good at front-end work. So, I actually used it inside Work Buddy to build a design studio website and a creator analytics dashboard. I also installed Impeccable, which is one of the design skills I've covered before, and used it for the second example. I'll quickly show you how to get started, and then we'll look at what I got, how it looked, and what needed another pass. So, let's get right into it. Now, the free access is the main attraction here. When I open the model picker on my existing Pro Trial account, Deep Seek V4.1 Flash had a free now label and a 0.00 credit multiplier. So, the app was showing zero credit pricing for this model during the offer. Their regular free plan also lists 100 monthly credits and a limited-time daily activity reward of 30 credits, but those are the general plan allowances. The Deep Seek promotion is the separate zero credit offer, which is what you want to select for this. For trying actual builds, that's a really good credit situation. I was able to generate both examples and ask for a refinement without hitting a usage limit message during these tests. I couldn't verify an exact daily request cap, though, so don't read zero credit pricing as a promise of unlimited requests. And this is a 2-week promotion, so check that the free label is still there when you're watching. Anyway, setting it up is pretty simple. Go to workbuddy.ai, download the international app for your computer, and sign in. Once you're inside, open a new task and click the model selector beside the message box. Select Deep Seek V4.1 Flash directly, and check for that free now label. For this route, you don't need to configure your own Deep Seek API key. Then, describe what you want to build, give it a separate project folder to save the files in, and send the task. That's basically it. Now, for the first example, I asked it to build a portfolio website for a fictional design studio called Forma. I gave it a clear visual direction, a warm ivory background, oversized typography, burnt orange accents, and some architectural artwork. I also asked for a project grid, category filters, a mobile menu, and a light and dark theme switch. So, this is what it generated. The first thing I liked was the typography. It used this very large serif headline, "Form follows feeling", with the last word in orange italics. There was a lot of space around it, and the artwork on the right used an arch, a staircase, and a sunlight shape. It had a proper editorial feel. The colors, the type, and the illustrations looked like they belonged to the same studio. And it generated the artwork as vector graphics inside the page, so I didn't have to go and find a bunch of stock images for this example. When I scrolled down, it had created eight fictional projects with different illustrations. The project grid was staggered with different card sizes and positions, which gave the page some character. It also added services, a studio section, and contact information further down. I checked the interactions as well. When I selected spaces, the grid changed from eight projects to the two relevant projects. Selecting all brought everything back. I switched the theme, and the page changed from that warm paper look to a dark palette while keeping the orange accents. I also checked it at a phone-sized width. The projects stacked vertically, the mobile menu opened, and selecting services took me to that section and closed the menu. So, the basic interactions worked, too. Now, this was still a front-end prototype. The project pages and social links were placeholders, and the studio details were fictional. But as a starting design that I could actually open and interact with, I liked it a lot. This was pretty good, for sure. And this is where design skills become interesting. I've already covered tools like front-end design, Impeccable, and Hallmark on the channel. They give the agent more specific guidance about things like typography, spacing, visual hierarchy, and how to review its own work. So, you can potentially combine that kind of guidance with Deep Seek's front-end ability, and get some really cool designs. The skill gives it a process to follow and your brief tells it what the design should feel like. In this case, I found Impeccable directly inside Work Buddy. I opened Experts, Skills, and Connectors, went to Skills, searched for Impeccable, and clicked install. Once it was enabled, I started another task and explicitly asked it to use the installed skill. For this second example, I asked for a fictional creator analytics dashboard called Signal. I wanted a completely different style this time. A dark graphite background, bright lime accents, compact typography, a narrow sidebar, and charts showing video performance. Work Buddy loaded the Impeccable skill and its responsive design guidance before building the page. It generated the dashboard with a views chart, traffic sources, a video table, small trend charts, and a sample insight panel. The overall direction felt more like a technical monitoring tool, which was what I was going for, but the first render had a noticeable problem. The metric cards were stacked down the left side of a big panel with a lot of empty space on the right. So, I sent that back to Work Buddy and asked it to fix the layout. I also asked it to change the live badge to demo because the numbers were fictional. After that pass, the four metrics sat in a compact row across the top with the main chart underneath and the traffic breakdown beside it. The demo label was fixed, too. It looked much more balanced and the lime chart lines stood out nicely against those dark panels. I didn't manually rewrite the code for either example. I gave Work Buddy the brief and then feedback on what I saw. I tested the range controls in the table search, too. Switching from 30 days to 7 days changed the chart and the numbers, and the 90-day view worked as well. Searching for Voxel narrowed the video table down to the matching entry. I also switched it to the light theme and the chart changed to darker green lines that were easier to see on the pale background. The dashboard was still using sample data and the extra sidebar sections weren't complete pages, so you would have more work to do before using it as a real analytics product. But it gave me a visual direction and working interface elements that I could build on. Personally, the Pharma portfolio was my favorite of the two. That large typography, warm background, and geometric artwork came together really nicely. The dashboard also showed why I like the design skill workflow, but it needed a feedback pass. Installing a skill doesn't mean you can skip looking at the result. So, if you're trying this yourself, give it a specific project and a specific visual direction. Say who the page is for, what should stand out, and which buttons need to work. Then, open what it generates, click through it, and tell it exactly what needs changing. For students, people learning front-end development, or anyone who wants to experiment with a few different designs, this free window is a useful opportunity. You can try the model inside an app that writes the files and works through the task, and you can add design guidance through skills as well. I'll leave the Work Buddy link and the related design skills videos below. Just make sure Deep Seek V4.1 flash is selected, and the free offer is still showing in your app. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, [music] consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, [music] give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: SWE-2 (Fully Tested): WHAT? IT ACTUALLY BEATS ASTRA & FABLE!
items.summary:
In this video, I’ll be testing Cognition’s new SWE 2 coding model to see how well it performs on KingBench 3, longer agentic tasks, interactive simulations, 3D applications, games, and model fine-tuning. I’ll also compare SWE 2 with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, discuss its clarification problem, and explain why its inclusion in the $20 Devin Pro plan makes it an interesting AI coding option.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 SWE 2 scored 67 out of 80, or 83.75%, on KingBench 3.
⚔️ It narrowly beat DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which scored 81.25%.
🏆 SWE 2 currently ranks fifth on the KingBench 3 leaderboard.
🧠 The model performed especially well on longer, connected tasks involving fine-tuning and local web applications.
📈 SWE 2 finished ahead of Kimi K3, Opus 5, and Fable 5 in this benchmark.
❓ Its biggest drawback is that it often asks too many clarification questions before starting the work.
💸 SWE 2 is currently included at no additional cost with the $20 Devin Pro plan through October 10, 2026.
👍 Overall, SWE
items.author: AICodeKing

In this video, I’ll be testing the newly launched DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with thinking enabled at maximum effort. It achieved 81.25 percent on my KingBench 3 coding tests while generating an estimated 221 tokens per second, including reasoning. I’ll cover its new architecture, benchmark results, API pricing, coding performance, and major improvements over my original thinking-disabled test.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash introduces a new architecture, native visual understanding, and lower API pricing.
🧠 Enabling thinking at maximum effort increased my KingBench 3 score from 53.75 to 81.25 percent.
⚡ OpenCode records suggest an estimated generation speed of around 221 tokens per second, including reasoning.
🏗️ The model uses a 552-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone alongside 196 billion Engram memory parameters.
